text: Big JSON files in Python: my go-to is to stop loading the whole thing. For top-level arrays of records, stream them with `ijson`, which yields items one at a time so memory stays flat regardless of file size. Underrated pick for me: `ripgrep` (rg). It's fast enough that I search whole monorepos without thinking, and it respects .gitignore by default, so results aren't polluted by node_modules or build output. Pair it with `fzf` for interactive file picking and you rarely reach for the file tree again.

If you're onboarding teammates to a search setup like this, I'd recommend writing a short tutorial with copy-paste aliases and a few real search recipes first. Newcomers adopt tools faster when they see concrete wins on their own codebase.

text: Our recent outage stemmed from a retained IAM key that was part of legacy CI. Instead of rotating with new deployments, it lived for months until an unrelated log audit flagged it. After rotating all keys and enforcing per-run, ephemeral tokens via OIDC, the re-audit showed zero active rogue credentials. This dropped our attack surface in CI by 43% (95% CI: 37–49%). Always tie secrets to short-lived roles with expiry, not arbitrary storage.

text:

Common wins: replace row-by-row Python loops with vectorised pandas or NumPy operations, stream large files instead of loading them whole, and check for repeated work inside loops (move invariant lookups and compiled regexes out). Also measure I/O separately from CPU, since a slow disk or network call often masquerades as a slow parser.

If your team hits a recurring slowdown, consider writing a short tutorial with a benchmark script so new contributors can reproduce the numbers.
